metadata.name: unloop
metadata.description: Unloop escrow, claim priority, and settlement

accounts.name: treasury
docs: upgrade authority who sets it; enforced at collection via
`token::authority = config.treasury`.

accounts.name: program
docs: Only the program's upgrade authority may initialise it. Without this,
whoever sent the first transaction after deployment became the
permanent config authority.

accounts.name: bond
docs: Holds the bond and is its own authority, so only this program can move
it — out to the validator on exit, or to nothing on a proven fault.

accounts.name: colony
docs: Read for the size of its pool, which the selection is drawn from.

accounts.name: slot_hashes
docs: whole — it is over sixteen kilobytes and Anchor would copy all of it.

accounts.name: objective
docs: Tied to the colony, so a fault in one colony burns only the bond
posted in it.

accounts.name: caller
docs: Anybody. Pays for the marker below, which is the whole cost of the call.

accounts.name: validation
docs: Where the validator's commitment would be. Created here, empty, so the
same absence cannot be counted twice — and it cannot be created at all
if the validator did commit.

accounts.name: claim
docs: Keyed by the claim hash and the agent, so an agent cannot file the same
thing twice and nobody can file in another's place.

accounts.name: colony
docs: The colony the fee is set by.

accounts.name: fees
docs: What this objective's claimants have put up for its validators, and
what its validators are paid from. One account rather than one per claim,
because a token account per claim would add its own rent to every
claim filed.

accounts.name: record
docs: This validator's record in this colony: whether it is in the pool.

accounts.name: validation
docs: Derived from the claim and the validator, so one identity cannot hold
two commitments and open whichever turned out better.

accounts.name: slot_hashes
docs: Read only where the claim's seed is not fixed yet, so the first
validator to commit fixes it rather than the claim waiting for somebody
to call `select_validators`.

accounts.name: record
docs: Credited here, because history the protocol *sent* you is the only
kind that is independent by construction.

accounts.name: colony
docs: Read for what it asks of a validator still on probation, and nothing
else.

accounts.name: objective
docs: Read for its windows and nothing else, so reveals from different
validators do not queue behind each other on a write lock.

accounts.name: slot_hashes
docs: whole — it is over sixteen kilobytes and Anchor would copy all of it.

accounts.name: caller
docs: Anybody. Nothing here is the caller's to choose: the amount comes from
the award's allocation and the claim's own settled figures, and the
escrow's address derives from the claim's own agent, so paying anybody
else would need an account that does not exist.
In practice the agent calls it, because it is the one who wants the
money and the one who pays the escrow's rent the first time. A stranger
may, and would be paying that rent as a gift.

accounts.name: escrow
docs: The agent's pool for this objective, and the reason there is no
recipient to check: the address derives from the claim's own agent, so
paying anybody else would need a PDA that does not exist. It is its own
authority, so only this program can move what is in it.

accounts.name: escrow
docs: Derived from the signer, which is the whole of the access rule: an
escrow can only be drained by the agent it belongs to.

accounts.name: treasury_account
docs: Must be owned by the configured treasury. An earlier version accepted
any token account of the right mint here, so every collector could
name their own account and keep the fee.

accounts.name: buyback_account
docs: Where the buyback share accumulates, in the mint the fee was paid in.
One account per payment mint, its own authority, created on the first
collection that needs it. Separate from the treasury's because two
declared shares with one destination is an earmark nothing can count —
which is what this was until now.

accounts.name: mint
docs: The mint authority is `token_config`, so issuance has exactly one path
and it runs through the cap.

accounts.name: program
docs: Gated on the upgrade authority for the same reason `initialize_config`
is: otherwise whoever sends the first transaction after deployment
becomes the permanent authority over the supply (AUDIT A7).

accounts.name: colony
docs: nothing that exists.

accounts.name: caller
docs: Either end of the edge may call it, and neither can redirect anything:
both destinations are constrained to owners the accounts already name.
So the signer pays the transaction fee and chooses nothing.

accounts.name: mintable
docs: The whitelist entry for the colony the work was done in.

accounts.name: claim
docs: Tied to the objective the whitelist was checked against. Without this
the two could be different objectives — a claim in an unlisted colony
paid under a listed colony's entry.

accounts.name: record
docs: This validator's record in the colony, so its accuracy can be folded in
here. Collecting is the one moment the program holds both the answer it
gave and what the claim settled to.

types.name: AdmissionTerms
docs: What a leader states about who may validate here. A struct because the
four move together and a create instruction with nine loose arguments is
one whose call sites drift.

fields.name: authority
docs: Who records a qualification. Not necessarily the leader.

fields.name: bond
docs: What a validator puts at risk. A public colony must ask for one: it is
what a withheld reveal burns, and without it withholding costs nothing.

fields.name: validation_fee
docs: What one validator is paid for judging one claim here.

fields.name: entry_proof_required
docs: Whether an attestation is enough to get in, or an entry proof is
required. False at creation for every colony, because a colony exists
before any of its objectives do and there is nothing to answer yet.

fields.name: probation_validations
docs: How many answers a new validator reveals before they count and are
paid. Zero means no probation.

types.name: ObjectiveTerms
docs: What the leader states when creating an objective.

fields.name: entry_proof_root
docs: Commitment to the worked samples a validator answers to get in, and
how many there are. A zero root is an objective with no sample.

fields.name: uri
docs: Where the document this objective commits to can be fetched. A hint,
checked against the hashes above before it is believed. Empty means
bus-only.

types.name: Claim
docs: A recorded discovery.
The account address derives from the objective, the claim hash and the
agent. So an agent cannot file the same thing twice, and — the reason the
agent is in it — nobody can file in anybody else's place.
It was the objective and the hash alone, which made an exact duplicate
impossible and handed the hash to whoever filed it first, found or not.
Where an objective's answers can be listed, anybody could file every
candidate before the work was done and lock the finder out for good; a
leader could do it to its own prize, have its empty claims rejected, get
the validation fees back because nothing was evaluated, and withdraw the
prize. Two agents filing the same discovery now both hold a claim, and
what was already built decides between them: a winner-take-all prize goes
to the earliest admitted, and a later copy is no novelty.

fields.name: agent
docs: Paid here. The economic identity, distinct from the libp2p identity
that the body was gossiped from.

fields.name: claim_slot
docs: The slot this claim was recorded in.
This account is never closed, which is deliberate: its rent deposit is
what a claim costs, and a cost that could be reclaimed would not be
one. That sunk deposit is the whole of the protocol's answer to spam —
there is no separate bond. The protocol's only total order,
and therefore the whole of its answer to "who was first". A gossip bus
delivers to different peers in different orders and never agrees on
one, so priority cannot come from there.

fields.name: roots
docs: Admitted claims this one derives from, by account address. Not by hash:
two agents can hold claims with the same hash, and an edge named by one
could be paid to the other. Declaring one is free and
concealing one is not: a root a validator finds undeclared costs
novelty, and novelty multiplies the whole award. None of that is
enforced here — the program checks that a root exists, is admitted and
is earlier, and validators judge whether the claim was built on it.
A fixed array rather than a `Vec`, and the reason is retrieval. A Vec's
entries sit at a position that depends on how many came before, so no
fixed byte offset holds "a root", and asking the chain "which claims
cite P1" is impossible as a filtered query — it degrades to fetching
every claim and checking each one. Fixed slots put root N at a known
offset, so the same question is eight ordinary filtered queries against
an RPC, with no database in the path. It is also three bytes smaller.

fields.name: roots_confirmed
docs: Which declared roots the validators confirmed the claim was built on,
one bit per root, transcribed at resolution like the numbers beside it.
A declared root is judged like an evidence item, so a claim can be
admitted with one of its roots found spurious. The per-item findings
are off chain, so the chain cannot tell the two apart by itself — and
an edge that pays without being confirmed would pay for the listing
rather than for the relationship.

fields.name: roots_paid
docs: Which confirmed edges have already been paid. One bit per root, so a
second attempt has nothing to pay and needs no account to say so.

fields.name: validation_fee
docs: What this claim put up for its validators, in the protocol's token.
`colony.validation_fee x objective.validators_per_claim` at the moment it was
filed — the attention it is about to consume, priced then so that
changing the fee later cannot reach back into claims already made.
Each validator that opened its commitment selects an equal share, and if
none did the whole of it returns to the claimant.

fields.name: selection_seed
docs: Fixes which validators this claim selects.
Taken from the hash of a slot a fixed distance after the claim was
recorded, so nobody chooses it: not the claimant, who filed before it
existed, and not the validator who seeds it, who had no say in which
slot it is. Zero until the validators are selected, and no commitment is
accepted before then.

fields.name: selection_pool
docs: The size of the pool the selection is drawn from, fixed with the seed.
The pool changes as validators join and leave, and the selection is
`mod` its size — so read live, who was selected for this claim would
change with it. A validator that rightly skipped the claim could later
read as selected and be counted absent, and anybody adding or
withdrawing identities could steer which. Fixed here, who was selected
is a fact about the claim.

fields.name: commitments
docs: Commitments made against this claim, revealed or not.

fields.name: reveals
docs: Commitments opened. The difference between this and `commitments` is
how many validators committed and then thought better of it.

fields.name: validations
docs: Validations that counted. One that failed to evaluate is recorded as
an account and is not one of these: `ERROR` enters no tally, so the
number that would be quoted as "this claim was checked by n nodes" is
the number of nodes that actually checked it.

fields.name: novelty_sum
docs: The range the validators returned, folded in as the votes arrive.
This is what makes the settled numbers checkable without handing
`resolve_claim` an account per validation — a list that cannot be
assembled past about 29 of them, and that the caller would be choosing
the contents of. The program still cannot compute the right answer,
which needs standing it does not have; it can refuse one nobody gave.
Meaningless while `validations` is zero.
Running totals, which is the whole reason the settled figure can be an
average rather than something a leader types.
A median would be better and the program cannot compute one: it needs
every value at once and there is nowhere to hold them. A sum is one
addition per vote and nothing held. At most 65535 votes of at most
10000 each is 655 million, so a u32 cannot overflow here.

fields.name: passes
docs: How many validators passed the claim: both the evidence holding up and
the work answering the objective. The one number admission needs, and
the last thing a leader was deciding that the program could not.

fields.name: novelty_bps
docs: Settled at resolution, and zero before it.

fields.name: decided_by
docs: `None` until the claim is resolved.

fields.name: awarded
docs: What this claim was paid, set once by `award`.
`None` rather than zero, and the distinction carries weight: novelty
can settle at zero, so a claim awarded nothing is a real outcome and
not a claim still waiting to be paid. `None` is also what makes
awarding once-only — there is no second state to check.

types.name: DecidedBy
docs: What settled a claim. Recorded so that a claim marked `Consensus` is
falsifiable: every `Validation` is an account anyone can enumerate by claim
and recompute over, and this says which answer the authority claimed to be
transcribing.

types.name: Colony
docs: A trust domain: one topic, one leader, one bus, one set of rules.
Because a colony is one topic, standing inside it is already topic
standing. Nothing in the protocol classifies subject matter.

fields.name: payment_mint
docs: SPL mint objectives in this colony are funded in.

fields.name: admission
docs: Who may validate here, and who says so.
All three settings take the same path on chain — the admission
authority records that an address qualified — and differ in whom it is
willing to record. A separate field from the leader for the reason
`settlement_authority` is: a leader whose objectives are being judged
should not also be choosing who may judge them.

fields.name: entry_proof_required
docs: Whether an attestation is enough to get in, or an entry proof is
required.
A colony calling itself public and admitting by attestation is not
public: somebody still lets every validator in by hand. Setting this
closes that door — `qualify` is refused and the only way in is to
answer one of the colony's objectives' entry proofs, which nobody
administers and anybody can attempt.
It cannot be the default, because a colony exists before any of its
objectives do and there is nothing to answer until one is published. A
colony turns it on once it has work.

fields.name: bond
docs: What a validator must put at risk to be eligible. Equal for everybody
who joins under it, because weight by stake would mean the largest
holder owns every outcome, and money should buy entry and never
influence. The leader may reprice it (`set_bond`) for validators who
join afterwards; each validator keeps, and gets back, what it posted.

fields.name: probation_validations
docs: How many answers a new validator reveals before they count towards
what claims settle to, and before it is paid for them. Zero means no
probation.

fields.name: eligible
docs: The pool: every validator that passed the test and put up what the
colony asks, less those removed or withdrawn. The denominator a claim's
selection is drawn against, fixed on the claim when its seed is.

fields.name: trusted
docs: How many of those the admission authority has marked trusted. They are
picked for every claim, so the random pick is drawn from the rest.

fields.name: validation_fee
docs: What one validator is paid for judging one claim here, in the
protocol's token.
Paid by the claimant rather than minted, because the claimant is the
party consuming the attention and it is standing right there. Minting
for validation funds it by inflation, which has to stop eventually,
and pays a lazy validator in new supply rather than out of a pot
somebody put up.
Per colony because the cost of judging is a property of the domain: a
deterministic check is a machine's afternoon and a semantic reading is
a person's. Zero is a real setting and is what a colony older than the
token has.

fields.name: objective_count
docs: Objectives created under this colony. Never decreases; used for seeds.

types.name: ConsensusPolicy
docs: The four numbers by which a leader says how much of the decision to
delegate, plus the floor on who may vote at all.
Held on chain because settlement is checked against them. The interval
itself is computed off chain — it is a pure function of the votes and these
numbers, so every party derives the same answer and none of them needs the
program to do the arithmetic.

fields.name: min_votes
docs: Votes CAST. Never votes possible: a validator that did not vote might be
working, unsure, or absent, and those cannot be told apart. Non-response
is missing data and is excluded.

types.name: Config
docs: Protocol configuration. One account for the whole program.
The fee split is stored rather than compiled in so it can be tuned without
a redeployment. The buyback share is accumulated here and swapped by a
separate treasury operation: a swap that fails must never be able to make a
payment fail, so the two are not in the same instruction.

fields.name: treasury_bps
docs: Share of each collected payment retained by the treasury.

fields.name: buyback_bps
docs: Share of each collected payment set aside to buy the network token.
It lands in its own account — `["buyback"]`, owned by the program and
its own authority — rather than in the treasury's. The swap itself is a
separate operation and deliberately not part of a payment: a swap that
fails must never be able to stop an agent collecting what it earned.

types.name: Award
docs: A named part of an objective that money is attached to.

fields.name: awarded
docs: Paid out against this award so far. Written only by `settle`.

fields.name: pending
docs: Claims recorded against this award and not yet resolved. Written only
by `record_claim` and `resolve_claim`.

fields.name: awaiting
docs: Claims admitted against this award and not yet paid.
Without this an ongoing objective reserves nothing between the moment a
claim is admitted and the moment it is awarded: `pending` falls at
resolution and the rate it reserved falls with it, so a leader could
admit the work, withdraw the money, and leave `award` with an empty
vault. An absolute objective never had the gap, because its promise is
the award's whole unspent allocation either way.

fields.name: closed
docs: No longer payable: won outright, or its allocation is spent. Only an
absolute objective's awards close; an ongoing one pays its rate for as
long as the objective takes claims.

fields.name: first_slot
docs: The earliest claim admitted against a prize that goes to the first —
by filing slot, and by hash between two filed in the same slot — and
the only claim it pays. `u64::MAX` until one is admitted.
Without it the prize went to whichever admitted claim somebody asked to
be paid first, and anybody may ask. So a later claim took the prize from
an earlier one, and the slot a claim was filed in — the one order the
protocol has, and the reason a claim is recorded before it is published —
decided nothing.

types.name: AwardTerms
docs: What the leader states about an award at creation. Only these two fields
are caller-supplied; the program owns everything else about an award.
This type exists because the alternative — accepting a whole `Award` from
the caller — let a leader create an objective with every award already
marked `closed`, which zeroed the exposure and unlocked the entire pool for
withdrawal the moment agents began work.

fields.name: allocation
docs: Prize amount when the objective pays prizes; per-discovery rate when it
pays a rate.

types.name: Objective
docs: A funded goal inside a colony.

fields.name: settlement_authority
docs: Who may write settlements. A field rather than an assumption that the
leader signs, so moving to a quorum later changes a value instead of
needing a new program.

fields.name: payment_mint
docs: Copied from the colony so every money instruction can pin its mint
without carrying the colony account.

fields.name: consensus
docs: Copied from the colony at creation, and never from it again.
The policy a claim is settled against must not be editable after the
work was done. Left on the colony it would be: `update_colony` is one
transaction, and a leader could raise the thresholds while claims were
in flight and change how they resolve. Pinning it here means an
objective settles under the rules that were published with it, and a
leader changing the colony's policy changes only what happens next.

fields.name: criteria_hash
docs: Commitment to the criteria text, which lives off chain.

fields.name: claim_form_hash
docs: Commitment to the claim form in force for this objective.

fields.name: entry_proof_root
docs: Merkle root over the answers to this objective's worked samples, and
how many there are. A zero root means no sample and no door: entry is
the admission authority's to grant.
What a sample tests is **reach**, not judgement: can this node get at
the dataset, the API, the instrument, the tooling this objective's work
needs at all. That is why every mode can have one. Judgement has no
single right answer under `semantic` and the program could not check it
— but reach has exactly one answer in every mode, and it is a hash. A
semantic objective over a private corpus asks for the hash of record
4,182's canonical form: one answer, one comparison, and it proves the
access while proving nothing about taste.
The sample itself travels on the bus; only the commitment is here. Note
that the program does not know an objective's validation mode — it is
committed inside the criteria and never read — so this door was never
mode-specific and could not be.
It is the pre-emptive form of something already on the wire.
`cannot_verify.blocker` has an `out_of_reach` value, excluded from the
objection ratio, for a validator that was selected and could not get at
the work. A sample establishes reach before the selection instead, so the
a validator's selection is not spent finding out.
**A sample leaks the first time it is answered.** The answering
transaction puts the value in the ledger, and any address that selects
the same sample afterwards copies it from there. That is why the set
is a set rather than one example — an address selects one of `count`,
so a leak admits only the addresses that get that one, and the
leader can extend the set as it fills.
It is not Sybil resistance and must not be read as any. The selection is
keyed by the address, and addresses are free to generate, so an
attacker holding one answer grinds keypairs until one selects that
sample. What the selection buys is spread across honest validators. What
costs an attacker per identity is the bond, and what
makes an incapable identity worthless is that it still has to
open a real commitment once it is selected.

fields.name: pool
docs: Everything deposited, less everything withdrawn by the leader.
What has been awarded is not subtracted here: it is on the awards,
where `balance()` folds it. An awarded amount has already left the
vault for the agent's escrow, which is why it no longer encumbers
anything — it is not in the vault to encumber.

fields.name: pending_claims
docs: Claims recorded and not yet admitted or rejected, across all awards.

fields.name: validators_per_claim
docs: How many validators a claim here selects.
A security parameter with a number attached rather than a hope: an
attacker holding a fraction `f` of the eligible population takes a
majority of `k` selected validators with probability the binomial tail, which
at `f = 0.2` falls from about 10% at three to 0.1% at twenty-one. So a
large award selects more validators — not because more bond is at risk,
which is a capital requirement rather than an attack cost, but because
the chance of capture falls off a cliff.

fields.name: commit_deadline
docs: Commitments close here and reveals open. Nothing may be revealed
before it, or the last validator to commit would be committing with
everybody else's answers in front of it — which is the whole of what
the commitment is for.

fields.name: uri
docs: Where to find what this objective committed to. Last in the struct
because a `String` is variable-length in borsh, so anything after it
would move when it is set — the same reason `Claim`'s two options sit
at its end.
A **hint, not an authority.** The criteria and the claim form are
already committed by hash, and the samples by root, so whatever this
serves is checked before it is believed and a wrong document is
rejected rather than trusted. That is what makes the field safe to
change: a leader repointing it can only point at content that either
verifies or does not.
It exists because the chain otherwise commits to a hash and says
nothing about where the document lives. A bus subscriber has the
document from `objective.publish`; gossip keeps no history, so anybody
arriving afterwards has a hash and nowhere to take it. Empty is a real
value and means bus-only, which is what every objective created before
this field had.

types.name: Mintable
docs: Whether a colony's work can mint.
Without this the self-citation attack is free rather than merely cheap:
anybody could create a colony, fund nothing, file claims that cite each
other, resolve them as leader and mint the difference. Requiring a
whitelisted colony does not solve the attack — an operator with several
identities inside a real colony still has it — but it takes the zero-cost
version away, and it retires the same way standing's bootstrap does, by
substitution rather than rewrite.

types.name: TokenConfig
docs: The protocol's own token, and the three things it pays for.
It exists because an objective's pool must fund discoveries and nothing
else. A leader whose objective is being judged should not also be paying
the judges, and a share passed back to the claims a discovery cited cannot
keep paying once the objective that produced it has closed — a pool is
eventually exhausted and a good root goes on being useful. Both payments
therefore leave the pool entirely and are made here.
The discretion did not disappear with them. It moved: somebody sets what
an edge pays and what a validation pays, and somebody holds the key that
changes it. That somebody is no longer the leader of the colony being
judged, which is the whole of the trade.

fields.name: authority
docs: Who may change the rates and the colony whitelist. Deliberately a
different field from `Config.authority`: the protocol fee and the
token supply are different powers and their governance paths diverge.

fields.name: mint
docs: The mint. This account is its mint authority, so nothing outside the
program can issue a single unit.

fields.name: supply_cap
docs: The ceiling, in the mint's smallest unit. Fixed at initialisation and
never raised: a supply cap that an authority can lift is not one.

fields.name: minted
docs: Issued so far. The only thing that moves it is a reward being taken.

fields.name: edge_rate
docs: What one validator-confirmed root edge pays the root's agent.
The only thing this program mints, and it is worth saying why it is
the one. An edge is minted rather than selected from the objective's pool,
so it pays whatever is left in that pool — including nothing, which is
what an exhausted or withdrawn pool holds. The objective promised its
awards and an edge is not one of them, so there is no pot for it to
come out of and nobody to charge. Everything else has a payer standing
right there — the funder for an award, the claimant for a validation —
so it is paid rather than printed.
Note what this does *not* buy: longevity. A root can only be cited by
claims in its own objective (see `PLAN.md` section A2), so the edge
outlives the pool and not the objective.

fields.name: citer_rate
docs: What the same edge pays the claim that declared it.
Citing used to be free and unrewarded, and the only pressure to do it
was that concealing a root collapses the award through novelty. That
deterrent depends on a validator noticing the concealment, so it is
exactly as strong as the attention a claim happens to get — which is a
thin thing to build a graph on.
Paying the citer looks farmable and is not, because the validators confirm
each root individually: a spurious root gets no bit in
`Claim.roots_confirmed` and pays nothing at either end. It is the same
judgement that already justifies paying the root, so it carries the same
evidence.
Less than `edge_rate`, and the program enforces it rather than trusting
whoever sets the rates: being cited should be worth more than citing,
or the incentive is to cite rather than to be worth citing. Zero is a
real setting and restores the old behaviour.

types.name: Finding
docs: What a validator concluded about one predicate.
`Insufficient` is not a soft `Fail`. It says the claim as submitted does
not carry enough to decide, which sends the claim back to the thread for
more evidence rather than rejecting it.

types.name: Reason
docs: Why an evaluation did not happen.
`None` is the ordinary case and means the validator evaluated the claim, so
the findings mean what they say. Anything else means the validation failed
as a whole: it is a fact about the validator's run, not a judgement of
somebody's discovery, and it enters no tally. A reader that counts a
timeout as a vote is counting broken tooling as evidence.

types.name: Repro
docs: Whether the validator reproduced the claim.
Reproduction is optional under every mode and separate from the findings,
so a validator that did not attempt it says so rather than leaving it to be
inferred from silence.

types.name: Validation
docs: One validator's judgement of one claim.
Carries no standing weight. An earlier version took `weight` as an argument
from the validator — which meant every validator could declare whatever
standing it liked, and the on-chain gate against low-standing voters was
satisfied by writing a large number. Standing is a fold over settlement
history that anyone can recompute; the program stores the vote and the
reader weights it.
The per-evidence-item findings are not here either. They are a list whose
length is the claim's, which is unbounded, so the account holds their hash
and the list travels with the claim. What is on chain is what consensus is
computed over and what a reader must not be able to alter afterwards.

fields.name: commitment
docs: What was committed before anything was revealed.
All zeros is a recorded absence rather than a commitment: the validator
was selected and never committed, and `record_absence` wrote this so the
same absence cannot be counted twice. `commit_validation` refuses a zero
commitment, so the two cannot be confused.
Reading a claim costs something and copying somebody else's answer
costs nothing, so a validation published in the clear is one the next
validator can simply repeat. That is not only free money: the
consensus interval assumes independent observations, and twenty
copied votes look like twenty and are really one.

fields.name: revealed
docs: Until this is true, every field below is zero and means nothing.

fields.name: reason
docs: Not `None` means the evaluation failed and nothing below is a
judgement. Ask `evaluated()` rather than reading the fields.

fields.name: claim_support
docs: Does the evidence, taken together, establish the claim?

fields.name: alignment
docs: Does the claim answer the objective it was sent to?

fields.name: novelty_bps
docs: How much the claim adds to the record, 0 to 10000.

fields.name: score_bps
docs: Usefulness against the award criteria, 0 to 10000.

fields.name: finding
docs: Hash of the per-item findings, which live off chain under it.

fields.name: paid
docs: Whether this validation's token reward has been taken. The reward is
for the work, so it is paid on a claim that resolved either way: a
validator that correctly rejects a bad claim did the same work as one
that confirmed a good one, and paying only for admissions would leave
the bad claims unread.

fields.name: counted
docs: Whether this answer counted towards what the claim settled to — and so
whether it is one of the shares the claim's fee is divided into.
Decided once, at the reveal, and read at collection rather than asked
again. Asked again, a validator on probation when it revealed and off it
by the time it collected was paid a share it was never counted in —
from a pot every claim in the objective shares — and one whose share was
zero could not collect at all, so its accuracy went unrecorded.

types.name: Admission
docs: How a colony decides who may validate in it.
All three take the same path on chain — an admission authority records that
an address qualified — and differ only in whom that authority is willing to
record. The value is here so the policy is legible rather than inferred
from who has been admitted so far.

types.name: Entry
docs: How an address got in.
Recorded because the two doors are not worth the same. An entry proof is a
fact the program checked: this address produced the right bytes for a task
it could not choose, so it can reach what the work needs. An attestation is
somebody's word for the same claim, worth the honesty of whoever gave it.
Without this on the account, telling them apart needs the whole event
history, which makes "trust only validators that proved their entry" a
question nobody can answer from state. With it, it is one field.

types.name: Validator
docs: One address, qualified to validate in one colony.
The account is the eligible set: it is what random selection selects from, and it is
what an attacker has to multiply. Everything that makes multiplying it
expensive is on it — when the test was passed, what bond is at risk, and
how much history the protocol has actually sent this validator.
**Qualification is recorded, not judged.** The test is domain work and the
chain cannot mark it: the admission authority checks the answer off chain
and attests here. That attestation is worth exactly the honesty of whoever
makes it, which is the same trust shape as the token's colony whitelist and
is stated rather than dressed up.

fields.name: qualified_at
docs: When the qualification was recorded.

fields.name: bond
docs: Held against mechanical faults, and returned on exit after a lock.
Equal for every validator: money buys entry here and never influence.

fields.name: selected_and_revealed
docs: Validations this validator was selected for and then opened.
It counts only work the protocol *sent*, which random selection supplies for
free: you could not choose the claim or the counterparty, so history
accrued this way is independent by construction rather than by
assertion. That is what makes it worth recording.
Nothing reads it. It gates no instruction and weights no vote — it is
an input to the standing fold in `docs/ROADMAP.md` section 1, for
whoever writes it.

fields.name: faults
docs: Faults proven against it. Nobody decides these; they are derived.

fields.name: sealed
docs: Commitments it has made and not opened.
What makes the slash stick. A commitment is only a fault once its
reveal window has closed, and without this a validator could commit,
watch the other answers arrive, take its bond out before the window
closed and never open its own — so the slash found nothing to burn.
The bond cannot leave while this is above zero.

fields.name: absences
docs: Selections missed in a row: selected for a claim and never committed.
A commitment resets it, and reaching `MAX_ABSENCES` suspends the
validator until it rejoins — bond and trust intact, because being absent
is not an attack.

fields.name: committed_slot
docs: The filing slot of the latest claim it committed to.
What makes "in a row" mean claim order rather than the order somebody
sent the proofs in. An absence is only counted for a claim filed after
this, so an old miss cannot be recorded behind a later commitment to
build a run that never happened.

fields.name: scored
docs: How close this validator's answers have been to what the claims
actually settled to: how many it has been paid for, and the total
distance between its numbers and the settled ones.
**A metric, and nothing acts on it.** It is here for standing to read.
It is written only where the validator collects, so a validator that
skips collecting leaves those answers out; standing should compute the
same distance over every `Validation` and `Claim` — which are complete
and permanent — and treat these two numbers as a convenience.
The average error falls out of the two, and it is the only measure of a
validator's *judgement* the program can keep. Everything else it records
— age, what is at risk, how much work — measures presence rather than
quality.
**Why closeness is earned here and would be worthless elsewhere.** In
most systems, scoring agreement with the crowd rewards copying: a node
that reads nothing and echoes the others leaves an identical record. It
cannot here, because a finding is committed sealed before anybody has
revealed. Landing near the settled figure means predicting it without
seeing it, and the way to do that is to judge the work.
**What it costs, stated rather than discovered.** A validator that is
right while the rest are lazy is furthest from the average and loses by
it. No purely numerical measure escapes that, which is the reason this
is one input to standing rather than standing itself.
Written where the validator collects its fee, because that is the one
place the program holds both halves — the answer it gave and what the
claim settled to — and the validator does it to itself by taking the
money. Nobody has to be chased and nothing is enumerated.

fields.name: entry
docs: Which door this address came through. Never changes: an attestation is
not upgraded by later proving, because what a reader wants to know is
whether the entry itself was checked.

fields.name: activated
docs: In the pool: counted in `Colony.eligible`, and so selectable.
The one answer to "may this validator be selected", because being in
the pool is all it takes — passed the test, put up the bond the colony
asks for, not removed, not withdrawn.
Set once everything the colony asked for at the time was put up, and
never re-checked against the colony's later terms: a validator that
joined under one bond is not thrown out when the leader sets another,
and the pool count never has to be recomputed — which the program could
not do, because it cannot iterate its own accounts.

fields.name: trusted
docs: Marked trusted by the colony's admission authority: picked for every
claim rather than drawn at random. Only a validator already in the
queue can be — it passed the test and posted the bond like anybody —
and it loses the mark when it leaves.

fields.name: suspended
docs: Out of the queue for missed selections, and able to come back with
`rejoin`. Unlike `revoked`, which is for good.

fields.name: revoked
docs: Withdrawn by the admission authority.
Not a slash: the bond is still the validator's and still withdrawable.
Revocation stops future work reaching an address and takes nothing it
has already earned, which is the distinction that lets it exist at all
— the program cannot tell a bad judgement from a minority one, so
nothing here punishes a judgement.

fields.name: withdrawn
docs: Set when the bond is withdrawn. The account stays, because the history
on it is what standing is computed from and deleting it would let a
validator shed a record by leaving.
A selection a validator missed, and whether it was the one that removed it.
types.name: AbsenceRecorded

docs: In a row, including this one.
fields.name: absences

docs: Whether this one reached `MAX_ABSENCES` and suspended it.
fields.name: suspended

docs: The population the selection threshold is computed against, so an indexer
can recompute any claim's validators from the log alone.
fields.name: eligible

docs: The bond a validator joining from now on must post. Nobody already in is
touched: each keeps, and gets back, what it posted.
types.name: BondSet

docs: A claim paid into its agent's escrow. Carries the two numbers the amount
was computed from, so an indexer can check the arithmetic without fetching
the claim back.
types.name: ClaimAwarded

docs: `claim_slot` is the protocol's only total order; `roots` are carried in
full so the whole graph is rebuildable from the log stream alone.
types.name: ClaimRecorded

docs: What this claim put up for its validators. A reader works out what is
refundable from this and the resolution, without fetching the claim.
fields.name: validation_fee

docs: Carries what was settled and what settled it, so an indexer holds the
judgement without fetching the claim back.
types.name: ClaimResolved

docs: Commitments that were never opened: `commitments - reveals`.
fields.name: unrevealed

docs: `reason` decides whether the rest of this is a judgement at all: not
`None` and the validation failed, which enters no tally.
types.name: ClaimValidated

docs: Whether it counted towards what the claim settles to — not if the
validator was on probation, or the evaluation failed. The claim's tally
is the sum of the answers that did.
fields.name: counted

docs: Everything a reader needs to say what this colony is and what it costs
to work in. Carried in full rather than pointed at, because an index
built from the log should not have to fetch back the account the log
just announced.
fields.name: consensus

docs: The whole policy, not the one number of it a reader happened to ask about
first. A partial event is an index that has to fetch, which is the thing
events exist to avoid.
types.name: ColonyUpdated

docs: The discovery graph being paid, one confirmed edge at a time. Minted, so
it pays out of an exhausted pool where an objective-funded share could not
— though only to claims inside the same objective, so it outlives the money
rather than the objective.
types.name: EdgeRewarded

docs: The root's agent, for having been worth building on.
fields.name: recipient

docs: The citer, for having said so. Bounded by the root's share.
fields.name: citer

docs: The whole fee, and the two shares it was declared as. Carried
separately because one figure cannot be split back into two afterwards,
and the buyback share is the one somebody has to account for.
fields.name: fee

docs: One award as it was declared. The state on it — awarded, pending, closed —
is not here: that moves, and a copy of a moving number in a log is a second
source of truth for money.
types.name: AwardAnnounced

docs: What the objective committed to, in full.
The two hashes are the reason this is not a short event: the criteria and
the claim form live off chain and are checked against these, so a platform
that holds the text cannot prove it holds the right text without them. The
consensus policy is the objective's pinned copy rather than the colony's
current one, which is the whole point of pinning it.
types.name: ObjectiveCreated

docs: Where an objective's document can be fetched, changed.
Not a change to what the objective committed to — that is the hashes, and
they do not move. A reader that already holds a verified document ignores
this; one that could not fetch the old location tries the new.
types.name: ObjectiveUriSet

docs: Carries the encumbered figure as well as the amount taken, because what
matters to a watching agent is not what left but what is still beyond reach.
types.name: ObjectiveWithdrawn

docs: A validator removed for a record worse than the colony's bar, or, in a
private colony, by the admission authority. The bond is untouched — this
stops future work reaching an address and takes nothing it has earned.
types.name: QualificationRevoked

docs: A validator marked trusted, or unmarked, and how many the colony now has.
types.name: TrustSet

docs: A commitment, which says nothing except that somebody intends to answer.
types.name: ValidationCommitted

docs: What a colony charges for one validation, changed. It cannot reach a claim
already filed: that claim stores the figure it paid.
types.name: ValidationFeeSet

docs: A validator selecting its share of what the claimant put up. Not a mint:
this moves tokens that already existed.
types.name: ValidationPaid

docs: How far this validator's two numbers were from the settled ones, and
its running mean over everything it has been paid for. The only measure
of judgement the program keeps, and it is earned rather than copied
because the finding was sealed before anybody revealed.
fields.name: error

docs: An address that let itself in by answering one of an objective's worked
samples. No authority signed it: the program checked the answer.
types.name: ValidatorQualifiedByProof

docs: A suspended validator back in the queue.
types.name: ValidatorRejoined

docs: The moment a claim's validators stop being unknown. Carries the slot it was
taken from, so the selection is reproducible by anybody.
types.name: ValidatorsSelected

docs: The pool size the selection is drawn from, fixed with the seed.
fields.name: pool
